headline: Penobscot Bay Turns: Bass Tighten to the Bait, Pollock Take Over the Monhegan Ledges
subhead: The new moon's tidal shove squeezed bait into the coves and rivers, and the fleet is finding stripers, mackerel, and the first honest pollock bite of the fall.
body_markdown:
Forty years hauling traps out of Boothbay teaches you one thing about September in this bay: the calendar doesn't tell the fish anything, but the moon does. Every fall there's a week where the tide swings hard, the bait gets squeezed into a smaller box, and everything with fins in Penobscot Bay decides to eat at once. That week just happened.

The new moon on the 10th pulled the biggest tide swing we've seen since spring, and it did what a big new-moon push always does up here — it jammed herring and mackerel schools tight against the river mouths, the ledges, and the harbor mouths from Boothbay to Stonington. Bait doesn't have anywhere to hide when the current's ripping that hard through a narrow gut, and the bass know it. We flagged this pattern last week, said the bait would keep tightening under the building moon and the bass would start committing instead of just picking at stragglers. That's exactly what showed up on the docks this week — better numbers, better sizes, and fish actually staying on a school instead of hitting it once and scattering.

The Georges River mouth and the mouth of the Damariscotta have both been holding stripers on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current funnels bait out past the ledges and the fish stack up to ambush it. Guys working live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a chunk of pogy soaked on the bottom in 15 to 20 feet, have been doing better than the jig-and-drift crowd this week — the fish are eating bait, not chasing lures around. That said, a chartreuse-and-white soft plastic swum slow along the current seam off the Rockland breakwater has picked up a few keepers in the last hour of daylight, right when the light starts to fade and the bass lose some of their caution.

Mackerel have been thick enough around Boothbay Harbor and out toward Eastern Egg Rock that you don't need much of a plan — a string of small jigs, a slow drop through 20 to 40 feet of water, and you're into a school inside a few minutes most mornings. That's good news beyond the frying pan, because live mackerel is the best bass and bluefish bait going right now, and the puffin colony out at Eastern Egg tells you the same story the bait schools do — there's a lot of small forage stacked up in that stretch of water this month.

Bluefish have made a modest showing in the outer harbors — nothing like the blitzes farther south, but a few 2 to 4 pound fish have turned up mixed in with the mackerel schools off Boothbay and around the Cuckolds. Worth keeping a wire leader tied on if you're jigging for mackerel, because losing a mackerel jig to a blue mid-retrieve is about as common a complaint as you'll hear at the dock this week.

The better story for the back half of September is groundfish, and Monhegan is where that story's being written. Pollock have moved up onto the ledges on the tail of the ebb, feeding on top in that nervous, boiling way pollock do when there's bait pinned against structure with nowhere to go. Diamond jigs worked fast through the top 20 feet, or a topwater plug worked slow across a boil, have both taken fish in the 3 to 8 pound range off the north side of the island. That bite has been the most consistent thing going this week — not spectacular every trip, but dependable, which counts for something this time of year.

Cod and haddock are still a deeper-water proposition, and the fleet working the channels between Matinicus and the outer bay is finding both in 100 to 150 feet on diamond jigs and bottom rigs baited with clam. It's not the numbers game it was thirty years ago — nobody who's fished this bay that long is going to pretend otherwise — but there are still fish holding in those deeper holes off Matinicus and along the edges of the Penobscot Bay channels, and September through November has always been the better stretch to find them stacked up before the water gets too cold to hold bait.

Water's cooling the way it does every September, and that's pushing this whole zone into its usual fall transition — the striper window narrowing week by week as the bass start thinking about heading south, and the groundfish and mackerel picking up the slack as the more dependable targets. That trade happens every year about now, and there's no sign this year's any different.

For the next few days, look for the bass bite to stay strongest on the last two hours of the ebb at the river mouths and harbor mouths, especially early and late in the day when the light's low. The mackerel and pollock bite should hold steady around Monhegan and Eastern Egg as long as the bait stays pinned to those ledges, which it should through the week unless a hard blow scatters it. If there's a wrinkle coming, it's the wind — a few days of a stiff easterly would stir things up around the outer islands and could push the pollock off the surface for a spell. Barring that, this is about as good a stretch as Midcoast Maine offers before the fall run thins out the bass and leaves the groundfish and mackerel to carry the season into October.
